note: Shared by all stories. Each object is one small fact box.

objects.name: Thebes
objects.desc: Religious capital of New Kingdom Egypt, centre of the god Amun (Karnak, Luxor). The Merneptah Stele was found in Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank.
facts: The Israel Stele was found here by Petrie in 1896.
The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah (Libyan war, year 5) is carved at Karnak.

objects.name: Memphis
objects.desc: Old royal city at the head of the Nile Delta, a main administrative and military centre of Egypt.

objects.name: Pi-Ramesses
objects.desc: Royal residence founded by Ramesses II in the eastern Delta (modern Qantir), close to the roads to Canaan. Its size is debated, but it was very large.
facts: Starting point for armies going to Canaan along the Ways of Horus.

objects.name: Napata
objects.desc: Egyptian-controlled town at the 4th Nile cataract in Nubia, the far south of Egypt's reach.

objects.name: Gaza
objects.desc: Egypt's main base at the end of the Ways of Horus.
facts: Major Egyptian logistical hub in the 13th century BC.

objects.name: Ashkelon
objects.desc: Coastal Canaanite city. Named on the Merneptah Stele: 'Ashkelon has been carried off'.
facts: Named on the Israel Stele next to Gezer, Yenoam and Israel.
Whether Merneptah really campaigned here, or the hymn is boastful, is debated.

objects.name: Gezer
objects.desc: Canaanite city where the coastal plain meets the hills. Named on the Merneptah Stele: 'Gezer has been seized'.
facts: Its king wrote letters to Pharaoh in the Amarna archive (14th century BC).

objects.name: Yenoam
objects.desc: Canaanite town named on the Merneptah Stele: 'Yenoam is made non-existent'. Where it was is not known for sure.
facts: Location disputed: Tel Yin'am, Tell el-'Ubeidiya and Tell esh-Shihab are proposed. Dot placed at Tel Yin'am.

objects.name: Megiddo
objects.desc: Canaanite city guarding the pass from the coast into the Jezreel Valley, on the main road north.
facts: Its ruler appears in the Amarna letters as an Egyptian vassal.

objects.name: Beth-Shean
objects.desc: Egyptian garrison town in the Jordan valley, controlling river crossings. Egyptian-style buildings and inscriptions were found.
facts: Permanent Egyptian base in the Ramesside period.

objects.name: Hazor
objects.desc: The largest Canaanite city of the Bronze Age, in upper Galilee. By 1207 BC it had probably already been destroyed by fire.
facts: Destroyed violently in the 13th century BC.
Exact date and who destroyed it are disputed (Ben-Tor/Zuckerman vs. Finkelstein).
The Book of Joshua says Joshua burned it.

objects.name: Jerusalem
objects.desc: Small hill-country town. In the 14th century BC its ruler Abdi-Heba wrote to Pharaoh (Amarna letters EA 285–290).
facts: Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem was an Egyptian vassal.
How large it was in the Late Bronze Age is disputed; little has been found.

objects.name: Shechem
objects.desc: Hill-country centre between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. Its 14th-century ruler Lab'ayu appears in the Amarna letters.
facts: Lab'ayu of Shechem expanded his power in the hills (14th century BC).

objects.name: Hebron
objects.desc: Town in the southern hills. Settlement was thin in the Late Bronze Age.
facts: Important in the Abraham stories of Genesis.

objects.name: Lachish
objects.desc: Major Canaanite city in the Shephelah (low hills), with Egyptian contacts. Destroyed in the 12th century BC, after this stop.

objects.name: Izbet Sartah
objects.desc: Small Iron I village on the hill-country edge. A pottery sherd with an early alphabet (abecedary) was found here.
facts: Founded around the late 13th or 12th century BC (Iron I).

objects.name: Timna
objects.desc: Copper mines in the Arava valley, worked under Egyptian control in the 13th–12th centuries BC.

objects.name: Tyre
objects.desc: Island port city on the Levantine coast, known from the Amarna letters.

objects.name: Sidon
objects.desc: Coastal port city, rival of Tyre.

objects.name: Byblos
objects.desc: Old port with close ties to Egypt; source of cedar timber. Its ruler Rib-Hadda wrote many Amarna letters.

objects.name: Ugarit
objects.desc: Rich port kingdom, vassal of the Hittites. Its tablets in an alphabetic script tell of grain shortage and enemy ships at the end. Abandoned c. 1190 BC, after this stop.
objects.people: Ugaritians (West Semitic), Hurrians and foreign merchants

pop.v: City c. 6,000–8,000 (one estimate near 10,000); kingdom perhaps c. 25,000–35,000

objects.name: Damascus
objects.desc: Oasis town at the edge of the desert; Egypt's northern frontier province (Upe) in the 13th century BC.

objects.name: Kadesh
objects.desc: City on the Orontes (Tell Nebi Mend). The great battle between Ramesses II and the Hittites was fought here in 1274 BC.
facts: Under Hittite control after the battle.

objects.name: Carchemish
objects.desc: Hittite viceroy seat on the Euphrates, governing the Syrian vassals.

objects.name: Emar
objects.desc: Trading town on the middle Euphrates, under Hittite control. Its tablets are an important archive. Destroyed c. 1185 BC.

objects.name: Hattusa
objects.desc: Capital of the Hittite kings in central Anatolia; huge royal archive of clay tablets, including the Akkadian copy of the treaty with Egypt.

pop.v: No reliable count. One estimate is c. 10,000–12,000; newer work suggests much of the walled area was not housing

objects.name: Troy
objects.desc: City at Hisarlik near the Dardanelles, probably Hittite 'Wilusa'. Level VIIa was destroyed around 1180 BC.
facts: Homer's Trojan War is a later epic tradition.

objects.name: Mycenae
objects.desc: Leading palace centre of Mycenaean Greece. Palace destructions in Greece came around 1200 BC.

objects.name: Assur
objects.desc: Old religious capital of Assyria on the Tigris, home of the god Ashur.

objects.name: Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta
objects.desc: New capital built by Tukulti-Ninurta I just upstream from Assur. He was killed here.

objects.name: Nineveh
objects.desc: Assyrian city on the Tigris with a temple of Ishtar; capital only centuries later.

objects.name: Babylon
objects.desc: Capital of Babylonia, ruled by the Kassite dynasty. Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria captured it and its king in the 13th century BC.

objects.name: Nippur
objects.desc: Religious centre of the god Enlil in Babylonia; many Kassite-period texts.

objects.name: Dur-Kurigalzu
objects.desc: Kassite royal city with a large ziggurat (Aqar Quf, near Baghdad).

objects.name: Susa
objects.desc: Lowland capital of Elam; temple of the god Inshushinak.

objects.name: Anshan
objects.desc: Highland capital of Elam (Tal-i Malyan in Fars).

objects.name: Chogha Zanbil
objects.desc: Ziggurat and temple city built by the Elamite king Untash-Napirisha in the 13th century BC.

objects.name: Nile
objects.desc: The river that made Egypt possible. The yearly flood fed the grain fields of the valley and Delta.
facts: Egyptian population depended on the cultivable flood land.

objects.name: Jordan
objects.desc: River running from the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea; a natural boundary between the western hills and Transjordan.

objects.name: Euphrates
objects.desc: Great river of Syria and Mesopotamia. In 1207 BC it roughly divided the Hittite sphere from Assyria.

objects.name: Tigris
objects.desc: River of the Assyrian heartland: Assur and Nineveh lie on it.

objects.name: Orontes
objects.desc: River of inland Syria flowing north. Kadesh lies on it. Drawn approximately on this map.

objects.name: Halys (Kızılırmak)
objects.desc: Longest river of Anatolia; it loops around the Hittite heartland and Hattusa.

objects.name: Karkheh
objects.desc: River of the Susa plain in Elam.

objects.name: Dead Sea
objects.desc: Salt lake at the lowest point on land, at the south end of the Jordan.

objects.name: Sea of Galilee
objects.desc: Freshwater lake in the north, fed by the Jordan.

objects.name: Mediterranean Sea
objects.desc: The sea linking Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus, Anatolia and Greece. Around 1200 BC, raiders and migrants called 'Sea Peoples' by modern scholars appear in Egyptian texts.

objects.name: Red Sea
objects.desc: Sea between Egypt and Arabia.

objects.name: Persian Gulf
objects.desc: Southern end of Mesopotamia; the 'Sealand' of Babylonian texts lay near its head.

objects.name: Aegean Sea
objects.desc: Sea of the Mycenaean palaces and the islands.

objects.name: Cyprus (Alashiya)
objects.desc: Copper-rich island, called Alashiya in Late Bronze Age letters to Egypt, Ugarit and Hatti.
facts: Identification of Alashiya with (part of) Cyprus is widely accepted.

objects.name: Sinai
objects.desc: Desert peninsula between Egypt and Canaan. The main road ran along its north coast.

objects.name: Negev
objects.desc: Dry south of Canaan; land of herders.

objects.name: Central hill country
objects.desc: Hills between Jezreel Valley and Beersheba. Around 1200 BC, many new small villages begin to appear here.

pop.v: 13th century BC: about 10,000 (our arithmetic: 50 ha × 200 people/ha, Finkelstein's density). Late Iron I: c. 45,000

facts: 13th century BC: c. 30 sites, c. 50 hectares built up.
Late Iron I (c. 1000 BC): c. 250 sites, c. 220 hectares.

objects.name: Jezreel Valley
objects.desc: Fertile valley crossing the hills; Megiddo guards its western entrance.

objects.name: Lebanon mountains
objects.desc: Mountain range behind the coast; source of cedar wood.

objects.name: Taurus mountains
objects.desc: Mountain wall of southern Anatolia between the Hittite land and Syria.

objects.name: Zagros mountains
objects.desc: Mountains east of Mesopotamia, between Babylonia/Assyria and the Iranian plateau.

objects.name: Syrian desert
objects.desc: Steppe and desert between the Levant and the Euphrates.

objects.name: Ways of Horus
objects.desc: Egypt's fortified military road along north Sinai to Gaza, with forts and wells. Shown in reliefs of Seti I at Karnak. Course drawn approximately.
facts: Line on this map is approximate.

objects.name: Coastal road north
objects.desc: The main road from Gaza through Megiddo and Hazor to Damascus. Often called 'Via Maris' today, but that Latin name is much later.
facts: The name 'Via Maris' is medieval/modern, not from 1207 BC.

objects.name: Israel
objects.desc: A people named Israel, the ancestors the Jewish people trace their name and heritage to. In 1207 BC it was a people, not a kingdom, and the Egyptians wrote its name with the sign for a people rather than a city.

pop.v: Unknown. The hill-country villages held perhaps c. 10,000–20,000 people around 1200 BC

facts: Named on the Merneptah Stele, c. 1208/1207 BC. This is the oldest known mention of the name outside the Bible.
Where exactly they lived and how they related to the new hill villages is still debated. Many scholars place them in the central hills.
Worship: there is little direct evidence for 1207 BC. Later Israel worshipped Yahweh, and how early this began is debated.
In the Hebrew Bible, Israel is the name God gave to Jacob, and his twelve sons are the ancestors of the tribes of Israel (Genesis 32; 35).

objects.name: Canaanites
objects.desc: Name for the people of the city-states of Canaan, each with its own ruler under Egyptian overlordship.

objects.name: Shasu
objects.desc: Egyptian word for tent-dwelling herders, especially in Edom, the Negev and Transjordan.
facts: A temple list at Soleb names a 'land of the Shasu, yhw'.
Whether yhw there is the god Yahweh is disputed.

objects.name: Egypt
objects.desc: Kingdom of the Nile under the pharaoh, the overlord of Canaan in 1207 BC.
objects.people: Egyptians; Canaanites in the vassal cities

pop.v: Egypt proper: c. 2.9 million (Butzer, for 1250 BC) to c. 2.9–4.5 million (O'Connor). Modern estimates

facts: Ruler: Merneptah, son of Ramesses II (reigned c. 1213–1203 BC; exact dates vary by a few years).
Held Canaan with garrisons at Gaza and Beth-Shean and the Ways of Horus road.
Gods: Amun, Ra, Osiris and many more.

objects.name: Hatti (Hittites)
objects.desc: Kingdom of the Hittites in central Anatolia, ruling north Syria through vassals. It collapsed soon after 1200 BC.
facts: King around 1207 BC: Tudhaliya IV or his successors Arnuwanda III and Suppiluliuma II; exact reign dates are uncertain.
Asked Egypt for grain in a famine; Merneptah says he shipped grain 'to keep alive' Hatti.

objects.name: Assyria
objects.desc: Kingdom on the middle Tigris, expanding west and south in the 13th century BC.
facts: Tukulti-Ninurta I (c. 1243–1207 BC) died around this time; his son Ashur-nadin-apli followed.

objects.name: Babylonia
objects.desc: Southern Mesopotamia under kings of the Kassite dynasty, recently humiliated by Assyria.
facts: Kassite kings ruled Babylonia for more than four centuries and adopted Babylonian language and gods.

objects.name: Elam
objects.desc: Kingdom of southwest Iran with two centres, Susa in the lowlands and Anshan in the highlands. Elamites spoke their own language; they were not Persians.

objects.name: Mycenaeans
objects.desc: Greek-speaking palace societies of the Aegean (Linear B script).

objects.name: Libyans (Libu)
objects.desc: Peoples west of Egypt. In Merneptah's year 5, the Libyan chief Meryey invaded Egypt with allies from the sea.

objects.name: 'Sea Peoples'
objects.desc: Modern name for groups named in Egyptian texts: in Merneptah's year 5, Ekwesh, Teresh, Lukka, Sherden and Shekelesh fought with the Libyans.
facts: Named in Merneptah's Great Karnak Inscription.
Where they came from and why they moved is disputed.

objects.name: Arameans
objects.desc: Not yet named in 1207 BC. First clearly named c. 1112 BC by Tiglath-pileser I of Assyria. Shown as a reminder of who comes next.
